crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research covers the use of AI systems that answer legal questions by first retrieving relevant passages from primary and secondary sources, then generating a response tied to those passages. The scope includes case law, statutes, regulations, court rules, agency guidance, and practitioner commentary across multiple jurisdictions. It is distinct from open-ended legal chatbots because every proposition in the answer is supposed to trace back to a citable document. The site's tracking of 210 compliance and regulation pages and 6,895 state AI bills shows the breadth of source material such a system must index to stay useful.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The system runs on a document store of legal texts, an index that supports both keyword and semantic search, and a retrieval layer that returns the most relevant passages for a query. Many implementations use embeddings, which are numerical representations of text meaning, to find passages that are conceptually similar even when they do not share exact words. A separate reranking step orders the retrieved passages before they are passed to a language model. The language model is then constrained to answer only from the supplied passages, and the interface displays the source citations next to each sentence.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A lawyer enters a research question, and the system breaks it into searchable components such as jurisdiction, legal issue, and fact pattern. The retrieval step pulls candidate passages from the indexed sources, often combining exact phrase matching with semantic similarity to avoid missing key authority. The generation step drafts an answer that quotes or paraphrases the retrieved text and attaches a citation to each claim. A human reviewer then checks that the cited passage actually supports the proposition, that no contrary binding authority was omitted, and that the law is still good law in the relevant jurisdiction.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are outdated or superseded law, missing negative authority, and leakage of confidential client facts if a query is sent to a third-party model. Provenance is handled by requiring every sentence to carry a source, a date, and a jurisdiction, and by logging which documents were retrieved for each answer. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which reflects the legal exposure around training data, outputs, and the use of copyrighted legal texts. The 210 compliance and regulation pages and 6,895 state AI bills indicate a patchwork of rules that a retrieval system must reflect without giving legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is moving toward real-time docket and legislative monitoring, where a system alerts a lawyer when a new decision or bill affects an existing matter. Agentic workflows will likely combine retrieval with document review and memo drafting, with each step verified against the underlying record. Jurisdiction-specific retrieval will improve as systems learn to weight binding versus persuasive authority automatically. The volume of state AI bills tracked on the site, 6,895, suggests that automated legislative tracking will become a standard part of case strategy rather than a separate research task.
